title: Alpha Hydroxy Acids
supports: AHAs may increase sun sensitivity; FDA's suggested label advises sunscreen during use and for a week after. Lists reported reactions (burning, redness, peeling), most often with heavily exfoliating products.

title: Allergens in Cosmetics
supports: Names fragrances, the EU list of 26 fragrance allergens, essential oils, methylisothiazolinone / methylchloroisothiazolinone, and formaldehyde-releasing preservatives (DMDM hydantoin, quaternium-15, imidazolidinyl urea, diazolidinyl urea, bronopol, sodium hydroxymethylglycinate) as common cosmetic allergens. Notes 'fragrance-free' and 'hypoallergenic' have no federal definition.

title: Fragrances in Cosmetics
supports: Fragrance ingredients can be listed collectively as 'fragrance'; people with fragrance sensitivities are advised to read ingredient lists.

title: How to safely exfoliate at home
supports: Prescription retinoids, retinol and benzoyl peroxide can make skin more sensitive or peel; exfoliating while using them may worsen dryness. Chemical exfoliation uses alpha and beta hydroxy acids.

title: Retinoid or retinol?
supports: Retinol is a retinoid sold over the counter; start slowly; retinoids can increase sun sensitivity, so use at night with daytime sun protection; retinoids should not be used during pregnancy.

title: Topical retinoids
supports: Topical retinoids can cause irritation (redness, peeling, dryness) and photosensitivity; adapalene is the least irritating and tretinoin the most; some are contraindicated in pregnancy.

title: Benzoyl peroxide
supports: Benzoyl peroxide is an oxidising agent; dryness and irritation are common; it bleaches clothing and bedding.

title: Chemical stability of adapalene and tretinoin when combined with benzoyl peroxide in presence and in absence of visible light and ultraviolet radiation (Martin B. et al., Br J Dermatol 1998;139 Suppl 52:8-11)
supports: In a lab study, tretinoin mixed with a benzoyl peroxide lotion degraded substantially under light, while adapalene stayed stable.

title: Topical Vitamin C and the Skin: Mechanisms of Action and Clinical Applications (Al-Niaimi F., Chiang N.Y.Z., J Clin Aesthet Dermatol 2017;10(7):14-17)
supports: L-ascorbic acid is unstable; formulations use low pH and stabilisers such as ferulic acid; ester derivatives (e.g. magnesium ascorbyl phosphate) are more stable.

title: Contact allergy to hydroperoxides of limonene and linalool
supports: Limonene and linalool oxidise in air into hydroperoxides that are much stronger sensitisers; both are on the EU list of fragrance allergens that must be labelled.

title: Allergic contact dermatitis to essential oils
supports: Essential oils are a recognised cause of allergic contact dermatitis.

title: Methylisothiazolinone allergy
supports: MI is a strong contact allergen (ACDS Contact Allergen of the Year 2013); the EU banned it in leave-on cosmetics and restricted it in rinse-off products.

title: Formaldehyde allergy
supports: Formaldehyde and formaldehyde-releasing preservatives are recognised contact allergens.

title: Contact allergy to propylene glycol
supports: Propylene glycol can cause irritant and allergic contact reactions in some people.

title: Contact allergy to cocamidopropyl betaine
supports: Cocamidopropyl betaine, a surfactant in cleansers and shampoos, can cause allergic contact dermatitis.

title: Contact reactions to lanolin
supports: Lanolin (wool alcohols) can cause allergic contact dermatitis, more often on damaged skin.

title: CosIng - Cosmetic Ingredient Database
supports: Official INCI names and listed cosmetic functions (e.g. humectant, emollient, preservative, UV filter). Used for ingredient names and function labels; plain-language descriptions in this repo are the author's summaries.
